Case Study 3: Wet Pacific - Colombia

Source: vignettes/case3_colombia_ecuador_choco.Rmd
case3_colombia_ecuador_choco.Rmd

1. Epidemiological Context: The Hyper-Humid Chocó & Pacific Basins

The Pacific coastal plains of Colombia form one of the wettest biogeographic corridors in the world.

Epidemiological challenges include: - High precipitation (>4,000 mm/year>4,000\text{ mm/year}) leading to chronic soil waterlogging. - Simultaneous circulation of arboviruses (Dengue, Chikungunya) and malaria (Anopheles albimanus and An. darlingi). - Complex river corridors with palafitic houses erected along tidal or fluvial floodplains.

2. Targeted Indicator Suite

Indicator Implementation Significance
IEV d4h_iev() Vectorial Stagnation Index: detects areas where flat topography (slope≈0\text{slope} \approx 0) coincides with persistent surface moisture.
VARI / EVI d4h_vari(), d4h_evi() Captures vegetation vigor from standard RGB sensors in high cloud-cover conditions where infrared may saturate.
TWI d4h_twi() Identifies natural hydrologic flow paths and subterranean water accumulation in lowlands.
IRHE d4h_irhe() Stagnant Turbid Moisture Index: differentiates clean flowing river channels from eutrophic, brackish puddles favored by vector larvae.

3. Workflow

3.1 Libraries & Elevation Models

We load raster and vector processing tools to model hydrologic drainage gradients from digital surface models (DSM/DEM):

library(drones4health)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

# File paths to UAV elevation and multispectral data
path_dem <- "data/choco_pacific/Ohuay_D.tif"    # DEM / DSM
path_nir <- "data/choco_pacific/Ohuay_NIR.tif"  # NIR band
path_r   <- "data/choco_pacific/Ohuay_R.tif"    # Red band
path_g   <- "data/choco_pacific/Ohuay_G.tif"    # Green band
path_rgb <- "data/choco_pacific/Ohuay_D.tif"    # Orthomosaic

3.2 Topographic Wetness & Slope Modeling

We derive topographic curvature and hydrologic wetness index (TWI) to locate flood basins:

# Compute continuous Slope (degrees) and Topographic Wetness Index (TWI)
r_slope <- d4h_slope(dem_raster = path_dem, unit = "degrees")
r_twi   <- d4h_twi(dem_raster = path_dem)

3.3 Stagnant Turbid Moisture (IRHE) & Vector Stagnation (IEV)

We isolate stagnant turbid moisture pools from active river flow and compute the integrated Vectorial Stagnation Index (IEV):

# Compute Stagnant Turbid Moisture (IRHE)
r_irhe <- d4h_irhe(red = path_r, green = path_g)

# Compute Vectorial Stagnation Index (IEV) merging NDWI and Slope
r_ndwi <- d4h_ndwi(green = path_g, nir = path_nir)
r_iev  <- d4h_iev(ndwi = r_ndwi, slope = r_slope)

Figure 3.3: Spectro-topographic detection of stagnant micro-basins and moisture accumulation zones.

3.4 Visual Analytics & Dual-Layer Inspection

We contrast topographic accumulation against stagnant moisture puddles to verify drainage conditions:

# Interactive side-by-side swipe comparison
d4h_mapview_swipe(
  x       = r_twi,
  y       = r_irhe,
  col_x   = "viridis",
  col_y   = "magma",
  basemap = TRUE
)

3.5 Executive Exposure Summary & Basin Indicators 

# Executive multi-moment summary across the surveyed river corridor
pacific_summary <- d4h_executive_summary(r_iev, by = "general")
print(pacific_summary)
#> ── Executive Summary: Pacific Corridor Stagnation & Moisture Exposure ──
#> Total Corridor Surveyed: 112.8 ha
#> Mean IEV Index: 0.472 (SD: 0.165)
#> High Stagnation Zones: 31.4 ha (Slope < 2° & Waterlogged Soil)
#> Critical Drainage Choke Points: 14 primary confluence sites
